easy.heading: Starting Off With Some Easy Math
easy.body:
Today's easy puzzle felt like a nice warm-up to get the brain moving. I started by looking for the biggest numbers on the board. That sum 15 region across the top right really caught my eye. Since the total is so high, I knew I needed to use my biggest dominoes there, like the [6,5] and [4,6]. It was just a matter of seeing how they fit together with the other pieces.

After that, I moved down to the bottom right where there was a sum 12 region. I placed the [5,5] domino vertically to cover the empty spot and help fill that sum. Once the big pips were in place, the smaller constraints like the sum 3 and the less than 5 regions were much easier to handle. It is always a relief when the last few pieces just click right into place without any fuss.

medium.heading: Finding Harmony in the Middle Ground
medium.body:
The medium puzzle today was all about balance. Instead of just adding things up, I had to deal with several equals regions. These can be a little tricky because they force you to find dominoes with matching pip values. I noticed right away that the [4,4] domino was going to be my best friend for the equals region in the middle of the board. Putting those matching pips at [1,3] and [1,4] made the surrounding areas much clearer.

I also had to keep an eye on the greater than 3 constraint at cell [1,0]. Since I had the [6,4] domino available, placing the 6 there was an easy choice. The rest of the puzzle felt like a bit of a dance, moving pieces around until the [0,0] and [2,2] dominoes found their homes. It took a second to make sure the less than 7 region at the top was satisfied, but once I tucked the [0,4] domino in there, everything balanced out perfectly.

hard.heading: Cracking the Code of the Big Zero
hard.body:
The hard puzzle today looked totally intimidating at first glance, especially with that massive region that had to sum to zero. But then I realized that a sum of zero is actually a gift! It meant every single cell in that five-cell zone had to be a zero. I grabbed my [0,0] domino and parts of my other zero-value dominoes like [6,0] and [1,0] to fill that area immediately. That one move cleared out a huge chunk of the board.

Next, I tackled the bottom section where there were multiple equals regions. I had to be careful with how I used the [3,3] and [5,3] dominoes to make sure all those connected cells stayed the same. The real breakthrough came when I figured out the [6,6] domino had to go near the bottom to satisfy the equals constraint across [5,3] and [5,4]. It felt like a giant logic chain where one right move led to the next. By the time I got to the top right corner for the sum 3 and sum 4 spots, I only had a few dominoes left, and they fit like a glove. What a satisfying finish!

explanation.tips: Try to look for the most restrictive rules first, like a sum of zero or a very high sum that requires your biggest dominoes. If you see an equals region that covers multiple cells, check your remaining dominoes for doubles or pips that appear frequently. It also helps to work from the edges of the board toward the center so you don't get boxed in.
explanation.learned: I learned that zero-sum regions are actually your best friend in the hard puzzles because they narrow down the possibilities so fast. It was also interesting to see how the equals regions can act as anchors that hold the whole puzzle together. Today really showed me that even when a puzzle looks complicated, breaking it down into small sections makes it totally doable.

faqs.question: How do you solve NYT Pips sum regions?
faqs.answer: To solve sum regions, look at the target number and the number of cells in the region. High sums usually require dominoes with 5 or 6 pips, while low sums like zero require dominoes with no pips at all.

faqs.question: What does the equals constraint mean in Pips?
faqs.answer: The equals constraint means that every cell within that specific colored region must have the exact same number of pips. This often requires using double dominoes or matching sides of different dominoes.

faqs.question: Is there a trick to the NYT Pips hard puzzle?
faqs.answer: The best trick for the hard puzzle is to look for regions that have only one possible combination of pips. Start with those certainties and the rest of the board will slowly reveal itself.

faqs.question: What is the best strategy for beginners in NYT Pips?
faqs.answer: Beginners should start with the easy puzzle to understand how dominoes bridge across different regions. Focus on the most extreme constraints first, like very large or very small sums.

faqs.question: How are dominoes placed in the NYT Pips game?
faqs.answer: Dominoes are placed in pairs of adjacent cells. Each domino can be placed horizontally or vertically, and each pip value can only be used once according to the set of dominoes provided for that day.
